title: Chapter 189 – The Tree
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door, the Dock, and the Mother Tree – Ethan]

The wire comes out of him on the thirty-first day of the snow, and Ethan Cole, who has not slept in six hundred years, falls asleep at once.

He does not feel it go. That is the strange part. For six centuries it has lain under the skin of his left wrist, a thread of silver as fine as a hair, tied to the great crystal that holds him over the shaft. He had forgotten it was there. He thought it a part of the chamber, like the cushions and the mist. But on the thirty-first night a tremor passes down the line, a long clear shudder, as if a fish had been taken from the other end, and the thread goes slack. A small cold quiet spreads up his arm. It is the first silence he has known since the year the loop began.

He sleeps. He dreams of nothing. When he wakes, the light in the shaft has gone from milk to a clear pale gold, and a hand is resting on his shoulder.

"Mr. Cole," says Nurse.

Is it morning?

"It is evening. You have slept two days." She is kneeling beside the crystal platform in her gray apron with a basin of warm water. Her cap has slipped, and wisps of white hair stick out round her ears. Her face is the same face he has seen every day for six hundred years, small and round and capable, and for the first time it looks frightened. "Something has happened to the beasts."

The beasts.

"The ones in the valley. The ones the Hall's old wire ran to. I can feel them in the stone, through the roots." She wrings the cloth. "They are going home. There are thousands. They have been singing for a month."

He looks down at his left wrist.

It is bare. The skin is white and smooth, as if the wire had never been. In the middle of it, where the thread went in, is a tiny round scar, no larger than a grain of rice.

Oh, says Ethan Cole.

He remembers. It comes in pieces, like snow sliding off a roof. A lantern in a white cave. A man kneeling in white fur. A cry, faint, ancient, down a long dark line. Thank you. He feels, in his chest, the echo of it, and he understands.

It was me.

"Mr. Cole—"

It was me, Nurse. All this time. His voice is a thread. The Veiled put a lead in the Moonhorn's heart. I did not know. I never knew. But the other end of it was in my wrist. Every time I was afraid, every time I woke at night and wanted to stop the Hall from failing, the beasts felt it. They came to the dark places because I was in the dark. I called them. I called them to the sleepers. I killed thirty-one of the children's neighbors on the night of the shed, and I never once knew.

Nurse puts down the basin. She takes his cupped hand, the transparent one, the one that holds the seed of light, and holds it in both of hers.

"You didn't know," she says.

That is not an answer.

"No." Her voice is thick. "But it is what I have."

* * *

Mei is awake, and she has been listening.

She is sitting in his palm with her knees drawn up and her chin on them, a small bright shape with a ribbon of silver for a body, and she does not look at him. She is looking at the wall of the shaft. Her face, in the gold light, is very still.

Papa, she says.

Yes.

I'm at nineteen.

He closes his eyes.

The shedding stopped, she goes on, in a small even voice, when the Alpha died. I'm not falling anymore. But I'm at nineteen. I didn't tell you. I wanted you to sleep.

Sweetheart—

I can feel it. The tree is calling. She turns her head. Her eyes are gray and clear and old. Not to take me. It never wanted to take me. It's been trying to tell me something for a hundred years, and I haven't been able to hear. The wire was in the way.

The wire?

It was your fear. It was so loud. A small wavering smile. It's gone now. I can hear her.

Hear who?

I don't know, says Mei. But she sings very well.

Ethan stares at her. A cold weight settles in his chest. He feels it the way he felt the first morning of the loop, when he woke in a world that had stopped being his: a vast, silent, falling certainty that he has forgotten something terrible and essential.

Nurse's lips press thin. "She has been listening to it every night. I thought it was the pipes."

What does it sing?

"No words." She looks at the wall, then at him. "But when it sings, the Hall's lamps lean toward the stair. All two hundred thousand of them. I have counted. Last night one of the sleepers in the third ring opened her eyes. Only for a breath. She said one word."

What word?

"Lena," says Nurse. "I did not know it. Do you?"

He does not answer. He cannot. The name lies in his mind like a stone at the bottom of a well, cold and smooth and without a bottom. He knows the shape of it the way a tongue knows the gap of a lost tooth.

"Mr. Cole?"

Yes. I think I do.

Nurse, he says again, and his voice is not steady. Is the door open?

"The sixth door? Only a crack. Mei opens it for an hour at a time."

I want to go to the tree.

"Mr. Cole. You cannot leave the crystal."

I know. He lifts his head. But I can send a pattern.

* * *

It takes the whole of the day, and nearly all the strength Mei has.

He explains it as best he can. The Gate is a copying surface. The Hall keeps a stored form of him, a working record, and the form can be projected through any open door, as Mei was projected to the Dock. It will not be a body. It will be a shadow with weight, a pattern with a pulse. It will look like him, and speak like him, and it will last only as long as the door holds and the girl pays. A day, perhaps. Perhaps less.

Mei says yes before he has finished.

It'll cost me, she says, calmly. Four percent. Five. I'll be at fourteen.

Mei, no—

Papa. She turns to him. When I said I wanted a choice, I meant it. You can't keep deciding what's safe for me. I want to know who's singing. Her voice trembles. And I think you do, too.

He does not argue. He has not argued with her since the night she told him she was afraid.

So they do it at sunset, on the bridge over the shaft, with Nurse holding his hand and the Hall's two hundred thousand sleepers breathing slowly in the rings of light above them. Mei sings. It is a thin high thread of tune, and the gold in the shaft leans toward it. A seam opens in the air, a tall narrow doorway of pale gray, and through it blows a cold clean wind that smells of snow.

Ethan stands.

He has not stood in six hundred years. His legs are the legs of a dead man, light and trembling and strange. He sways. Nurse catches his elbow. He looks down at his own body, thin, white-gowned, translucent, a ghost with a shadow, and sees his hands. They are shaking. They have always shaken.

Thank you, he says.

"Go," says Nurse. She is crying openly. "Go and see her. Whoever she is."

He steps through the door.

* * *

The Dock is empty, and the cold is like a blow.

He stands on the polished black floor in the blue light, with his breath smoking, and for a moment he cannot move. He had forgotten cold. He had forgotten that the air could be so thin and sharp, so full of the smell of stone and old iron. He had forgotten the sound of his own footfall on a hard floor.

Hello, he says, to no one, and the cavern gives it back to him.

A soft clatter, then, from above, and a voice at the head of the stair: "Who goes there?"

A broad red-faced woman in a quilted gown comes down the last flight with a spear in both hands, and stops. She stares at him. She is, he sees, perhaps fifty, with a scar under one eye and the blunt unhurried bearing of a soldier. Behind her, a tall one-armed man in the same gown has appeared, with a plain staff in a hand of grained pale stone.

Neither of them speaks.

I'm sorry, says Ethan. He lifts his empty palms. I did not mean to alarm you. I am—

"You're Mr. Cole," says the one-armed man.

Yes.

"Jian's described you." The man's voice is even. "He said you'd be older."

I am quite old.

"You look like a ghost."

That is closer to the truth. A small awkward bow. I have a day. Possibly less. I was hoping to see the tree.

The one-armed man considers him a long moment. Then, with an unhurried gesture that Ethan will remember for the rest of his borrowed hour, he bows, a deep formal bow, with his stone hand pressed flat to his breast.

"I am Tian Mo," he says. "Warden of the Stair. You are very welcome here, Mr. Cole. I will carry you if you like."

Carry me?

"It is seven hundred and one steps."

Ah. He smiles, and finds it hurts his face. Then I accept.

* * *

They go up through the Garden in the last red light, and he sees all of it.

He sees the Hall, with its rows of lit windows. He sees the courtyards full of children, the snow trampled brown, the long lines of people at the kitchen door. He sees a boy of five run past him, shrieking, with a rabbit under his arm, followed by a three-year-old in a quilted smock. He sees an old woman in a blue smock on the steps, with a black kettle, who looks up as he passes and goes quite still.

Qinghe, he thinks. The mother.

She does not speak. She only watches him cross the courtyard on the Warden's arm, and he feels her eyes follow him as one feels a hand on the back of the neck. When he is nearly past, she says, in a low voice: "Mr. Cole."

Madam.

"My son said he would not forgive you."

He was right not to.

"He is a stubborn boy." She lifts her chin. "But I have fed a good many people in a hundred years. I have never turned a hungry one away. If you are hungry, there is soup."

He stops. His throat has closed.

I have not eaten in six centuries, he says. I am not sure I remember how.

"Then you will learn." She turns back to the kettle. "Go and see your tree. I'll keep a bowl."

He goes on.

A small girl is sitting on the lowest step of the orchard path with her knees drawn up and her palms flat in the snow. She wears a patched quilted gown that is too large for her, and her braid has come undone. She does not look up as they pass. Then she does, and Ethan feels the look go through him like a needle through cloth.

"Mo Yan," says the Warden quietly. "She does not speak."

She is one of the Seven.

"The eighth of the old experiments' children, if you want to count so. Eight years." The Warden's voice is careful. "The healer Yue hears her through touch. She says Mo Yan has been telling her for three nights that a woman is waiting under the tree and is not angry."

Not angry, says Ethan. His mouth is dry.

The girl rises. She crosses the snow with the unhurried steps of a child who knows exactly where she is going, and takes his shadow-hand in both of hers. Her fingers are warm. He feels them with a clarity that startles him, the small knuckles, the chip of dirt under one nail. She gives him one grave nod. Then she lets go and walks ahead of them up the hill, and does not look back.

They follow her.

The orchard is a field of white. Snow lies deep on the stumps, and a faint violet twilight has gathered between them, and in the middle of it, alone on its little hill, the Mother Tree stands against the sky. He sees it from a long way off. He stops, and the Warden stops with him.

It's larger than I remember, says Ethan.

"You planted it?"

I think so. He frowns. I have the memory. A basement, a seed, a lamp. A woman's hands. But it is like remembering a dream. I cannot find the end of it.

"What woman?"

I do not know. He closes his eyes. That is what frightens me.

* * *

The tree sings when he touches it.

It is not a loud thing. It is the quietest sound he has ever heard, a long low murmur in the bark, in the roots, in the frozen air itself. It is a hum, and a cradle-song, and the rustle of leaves in a house at night. He lays his shadow-hand flat against the silver trunk, and the warmth comes up through it like a tide, and the song swells, and he knows it.

He knows it.

Oh, says Ethan Cole. Oh, no.

His knees give way. He goes down in the snow with his palm still on the trunk, and Tian Mo has him, one strong stone hand under his arm, but he barely notices. He is not here. He is in a small dim kitchen in a house at the edge of a city that no longer exists, at three in the morning, in the year Mei was five. A woman is standing at the counter with her back to him. She is small, with dark hair coming loose from a clip, in an old gray cardigan that was his. A child is on her hip, a drowsy child with a thumb in her mouth. The woman is humming.

It is a nonsense tune. It has no words. She made it up herself, the night Mei was born, because the baby would not sleep. It goes up, and down, and up again, and trails off at the end into a little falling sigh, and Mei used to say it was the sound of a cat yawning.

Lena, he says.

The song stops.

For a long time there is only the wind. Then, from deep in the wood, faint and slow and familiar, a voice, warm and a little hoarse, a voice with a laugh in it, says: Took you long enough, Ethan.

* * *

He does not know how long he kneels there.

The Warden withdraws, quietly. The snow falls. The tree stands over him, vast and silver, with the last of the sun in its crown, and from somewhere inside it, from a hollow between the roots where the black soil is warm, a shape comes slowly into being.

It is a woman. She is small, and tired, and fifty years younger than he, with dark hair and gray eyes and a mouth that is trying not to smile. She wears the gray cardigan. She is made of faint gold light and the pattern of bark, and when she steps out of the trunk she leaves no footprint in the snow.

Hello, she says.

Lena. It is all he can say. Lena, I—you died. You died in the spring. I held your hand.

I did. She sits down in the snow beside him, quite casually, as she used to sit on the kitchen floor. And then you did a remarkable thing. Do you remember? You didn't want to lose me. You never did take it well when I left the room. A rueful smile. You put a piece of me in a seed.

I... I don't...

You don't remember. I know. It's the cut. She touches his face, and it feels like warm wind. You and the others. When you built the Doors, you made a vow that no single mind would carry the whole. You split your memory in nine. You gave yourself the pieces that were safest. You kept Mei. You kept the grief. And you gave away the rest, the part about the seed, because you were afraid you would try to use me.

He stares at her. His mouth works.

I have been here for six hundred years, she says gently. Growing. Listening. Waiting for someone to ask me how I was.

Lena, I'm so sorry.

I know. She takes his hand, the shaking one. It's all right. I wasn't alone. There was a woman who came every evening and sat under my branches. She brought a kettle. She talked to me about her husband, and her children, and the price of rice. She never knew I could hear. A warm laugh, like wind in leaves. I have been very fond of her.

The cook.

Qinghe. The gray eyes shine. She is a remarkable person, Ethan. You should thank her.

He laughs. It comes out cracked and wet and helpless, and then he is weeping, great ragged sobs that shake the thin shadow of his body. She holds him. She does not say it is all right. She only holds him, a small gold ghost in a gray cardigan, as the snow falls and the last light fades from the sky.

* * *

There is more, says Lena, and her light dims a little, like a lamp when a door opens. I will tell you quickly, because the girl is paying for every minute you stand here.

Tell me.

The Seam did not begin as a wound in the world. It began as a wound in us. She counts on her fingers, as she used to when she planned the week's shopping. Nine of you built the Doors. Nine took the memory of one part of the work and swore to forget it. You took the seed. Ma Ruo-lin took the sums. The Ferryman took the road out. Someone took the name of the thing that came through first.

The Veiled, says Ethan. He does not know how he knows it.

A woman who loved her work very much, says Lena. She is the one who put the lead in the Moonhorn. She did it to find you, because she had lost the part of herself that remembered why. She has been walking the valley for six hundred years with a mark on her hand and no idea what it opens.

Then it opens something.

A door, says Lena. The seventh. Under me.

He looks down at the roots. The snow around them is thin and strangely clear, and through it, deep down, he can feel it now: a vast quiet weight, a pressure of nine million sleeping breaths.

I cannot hold it shut much longer, says Lena. I am a tree, Ethan, and I am tired. The Rest of All have been dreaming a long time. Some of them have begun to dream of waking. If the Veiled opens the door before the Nine agree, they will wake all at once, in a world that has no food for them, and they will be afraid.

How long?

Ten weeks. Perhaps eleven. Her smile is crooked and brave. You always did like a deadline.

* * *

The tree is not a cradle for Mei, says Lena, when he can hear her again.

Then what...?

It never was. She sits back on her heels, and the snow-light turns her hair to silver. I know what you thought. I know what the Hall said. Compatibility with the Keystone pattern, 0.91. It was a true number. But it was not the number you thought. She smiles. It is not the number of a vessel and a child. It is the number of a mother and a daughter.

A mother.

I am her mother, Ethan. I carry her blood. I carry her songs. The tree was not made to hold her mind. It was made to hold mine, and mine is the only mind in the world that could hold hers without pushing. Her voice is very gentle. Do you see? She would not be a guest in a stranger's house. She would be a child in her mother's arms.

But that's...

That's what she asked for. Lena takes his face between her hands. She said she wanted a choice, not a cradle. She was right. I am not a cradle. I am a person, and I have been waiting a very long time to be asked.

Ethan looks at her. He looks at the pale sad face he has kept in his heart for six hundred years, and the gray eyes, and the dimple at the corner of the mouth that is the dimple Mei has. He sees what he has been too frightened to see: not a machine, not a vessel, not a way to bring his daughter back.

A family.

She could stay, he says. In the tree. With you.

If she chooses it.

And if she doesn't?

Then she goes somewhere else. Lena smiles. That is what a choice is, my love. It is a door that opens in more than one direction.

His hand has begun to go thin. He sees it as he lifts it, the snow showing faintly through the knuckles, the edges gone soft like breath on glass. The pattern is running down. Somewhere under the earth a girl of nineteen percent is holding a door with everything she has.

I have to go back, he says.

Yes. Lena rises with him. She does not hold him; she only touches the middle of his chest, once, where a heart would be. Take this with you. It is the one thing the cut did not take.

A warmth goes into him, small and steady, the warmth of a kitchen at three in the morning. With it comes a single memory, whole and plain: a woman at a counter, a child on her hip, a tune with no words.

Tell Mei, says Lena. Tell her there is no hurry. Tell her the choice is hers, and that I will love her whichever door she takes.

I will.

And Ethan. The gray eyes are bright. Eat the soup.

He laughs, helplessly, and the Warden, who has come back through the snow without a sound, offers his stone arm. Mo Yan is waiting at the edge of the orchard. She takes his other hand. Together the three of them go down the hill toward the lit windows, and the singing follows them as far as the gate.

At the gate he stops and looks back once. The Mother Tree stands alone on its hill against the first stars, vast and silver and patient, and in its crown the lullaby begins again, soft and slow, rising into the dark. He understands at last whose voice it is that has been singing in the Garden for a hundred years, and why a cook with a kettle came every evening to sit beneath it, and why no beast ever touched its roots.

He lifts his face to it. And for the first time in six centuries, Ethan Cole sings along.
